signals.title: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
November 7, 2026

Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has released Kinference, an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. Kinference is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. It sits in front of a fleet of vLLM workers and decides where each request goes. It applies routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. For dev teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients, it targets the layer above the model server. The project is Apache 2.0 licensed on GitHub. The current release is v0.1.0-alpha.7.

## TL;DR

- Size: v0.1.0-alpha.7, written in Rust, Apache 2.0, configured through 5 Kubernetes CRDs.
- Runs on: any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster running vLLM. Buoyant’s benchmark used 3 L40S GPUs per pool.
- Performance: large gains on prefix-heavy traffic versus plain Kubernetes Service routing (self-reported).
- Best: median TTFT fell from 6.88 s to 0.31 s (95%) on a shared-prefix workload.
- Worst: no median TTFT gain on prompts without shared prefixes (6.92 s vs 6.83 s).

...

## How fast is Kinference in benchmarks?

Buoyant published a benchmark against plain Kubernetes load balancing. Each arm used 3 vLLM 0.31.0 pods, each on 1 L40S GPU. The model was Qwen3.8-27B-FP8. Load came from GuideLLM 0.8.1. The baseline was a ClusterIP Service, where kube-proxy picks a random pod per connection.

Unloaded latency results (median TTFT):

| Workload | Kubernetes Service | Kinference | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control (no shared prefix) | 6.92 s | 6.83 s | No significant difference |
| Shared-prefix | 6.88 s | 0.31 s | about -95% |
| Multiturn | 1.70 s | 0.59 s | about -65% |

Median end-to-end latency fell 45% on shared-prefix and 32% on multiturn. On control traffic, p95 TTFT still dropped from 21.46 s to 12.33 s. Buoyant attributes this to queue-aware balancing.

The capacity test measured goodput: requests per minute meeting a TTFT SLO. Peak goodput was 103.0 vs 14.0 req/min on shared-prefix, about 7.4x. On multiturn it was 82.7 vs 23.8, about 3.5x. The Service baseline never met the SLO at any tested concurrency.

These numbers are self-reported. The baseline is random routing, not another cache-aware router like llm-d or Dynamo. Buoyant also notes its SLOs (8 s and 4 s) suit offline agents, not chat.

signals.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct GPUs
signals.excerpt:
# Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct GPUs: Day-0 support and optimization

 Nov 04, 2026

# TL;DR

- Kimi K3.1 Pro, Moonshot AI’s open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model (2.8T total and 104B activated parameters, 1M-token context), serves on 8× AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with both ATOM and vLLM on day 0, from the released MXFP4 checkpoint and with its DSpark speculative-decoding draft.
- K3.1 Pro keeps Kimi K3’s hybrid architecture: 69 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers and 24 latent-attention layers over an 896-expert MXFP4 MoE. It adds a sparse indexer (DSA) to every one of the 24 attention layers, which selects 2,048 tokens of history per query. ATOM serves the indexed layers on its shared DSA path, with an FP8 index cache next to the FP8 latent KV cache
- ATOM: native KDA and sparse MLA kernels, the routed experts on FlyDSL’s MXFP4 grouped MoE, per-channel FP8 attention applied at start-up, and a DSpark draft that shares the target’s KV cache and runs as a captured CUDA graph.
- vLLM: memory-efficient sparse attention with decode context parallelism (DCP) for long-context serving, alongside a specialized decode path for low-latency interactive workloads
- Accuracy on Moonshot AI’s Kimi Vendor Verifier, at reasoning effort max: OCRBench 0.871 (Moonshot reference 0.872); tool-call JSON schema 0.991.

...

# Serving with ATOM

ATOM serves Kimi K3.1 Pro with tensor parallelism over the eight GPUs of one MI355X node, for text and image input, from the released MXFP4 checkpoint without conversion. With the DSpark draft loaded, each GPU peaks at about 199 GB of its 288 GB during start-up, and a single 1M-token request fits on one node.

...

PTPC FP8 attention: At start-up, ATOM re-quantizes the BF16 attention and dense linears to FP8 with one scale per output channel, with activations scaled per token at run time (--online_quant_config with ptpc_fp8): 559 linears per rank, done in about 2 seconds. The routed experts, the KDA convolutions, the vision encoder and the indexer-packed down-projection keep their stored formats.

...

vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs with the MXFP4 checkpoint and DSpark speculative decoding. Built on AITER and FlyDSL kernels, the ROCm implementation combines memory-efficient sparse attention with decode context parallelism (DCP) for long-context serving, alongside a specialized decode path for low-latency interactive workloads.

signals.title: Supercharging XLA-based inference: Announcing the launch of XLA Serving Engine | Google Open Source Blog
signals.excerpt:
### Supercharging XLA-based inference: Announcing the launch of XLA Serving Engine 

#### Thursday, November 5, 2026

Oleg Shaldybin

 and 

Monica Song

, Google TPU Software

Today we are excited to announce the launch of XLA Serving Engine (XSE), a general-purpose model export and inference runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem, open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 license.

We created XLA Serving Engine to enable a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow. Most ML engineers develop models using Python (with frameworks like JAX and PyTorch); however, some production serving environments do not allow Python due to operational and deployment complexity. XLA Serving Engine offers a solution by providing an API for engineers to export their ML models to an “XLA SavedModel” containing the StableHLO representation of their model’s function, which can then be loaded and executed by the XLA Serving Runtime.

This approach allows users to serve models (typically non-LLMs) directly in a C++ runtime, which enables high throughput at any scale and optimizes for low latency by removing the overhead of the Python interpreter. In our studies, we found that for short requests, XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of the best Python server we could build, and 8–36x that of a straightforward one, while using 30–70% less CPU time per prediction and a quarter of the memory.

Last year, we began deploying core components of XLA Serving Engine as part of Google’s internal load-bearing, production serving infrastructure. Today, XSE serves over 6 million queries per second and powers some of Google's highest-volume online inference pipelines, including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search, and parts of Gemini Omni, with plans to onboard more customers internally.

...

- Python-Free Serving: XSE enables a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow via the intermediary compiled XLA SavedModel serialization format. In our studies, we found that XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of a pure Python server.
- Low-latency execution: The XLA Serving Runtime wraps PJRT directly and optimizes the model using the XLA compiler. This eliminates Python runtime overhead and the global interpreter lock. XSE is C++ native, which means one process is capable of using all eight cores.

Figure 1: Throughput under latency target

- Orbax Checkpointing Integration: XLA SavedModel stores JAX model computations as StableHLO and uses Orbax checkpoint to store the weights.
- Flexible Scale: Supports both single-host and multi-host serving by leveraging PJRT.
- Performance Parity: XSE preserves the performance of the model’s forward function (including kernel optimizations). Hand off your model to XLA Serving Engine with confidence that performance will be identical to its training environment.
- Docker Packages: We provide a suite of Docker images that are tested on CPU, GPU, and TPU and expose simple gRPC APIs for calling your model.

signals.excerpt:
- FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and its distilled variant combine Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer, and an autoencoder to generate and edit images at high resolution.
- TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200.
- Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
- Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x.
- Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033.
- Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x.

...

FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers Base and distilled checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements.

This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads.

...

### Online serving endpoint

From the same container directory, launch the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/images/generations` endpoint:

```
cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen
trtllm-serve black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml

```

Once the server is ready, open a second terminal, enter the running container, and run the client:

```
docker exec -it tensorrt_llm bash
python examples/visual_gen/serve/sync_image_gen.py \
  --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 \
  --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \

signals.title: Zyphra introduces ZYFA : FlashAttention FP8 for AMD MI355X, up to 1.76x faster
signals.excerpt:
# Zyphra introduces ZYFA : FlashAttention FP8 for AMD MI355X, up to 1.76x faster

November 7, 2026

AI / news

Zyphra has released ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD), a set of FP8 and BF16 attention compute kernels designed for AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. According to the company, its FP8 kernels are between 1.16 and 1.76 times faster than AITER, AMD’s default kernel library, on real model activations. The code is released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license.

- Zyphra released ZYFA, an open-source set of FP8 and BF16 attention kernels for AMD MI355X GPUs.
- Its FP8 kernels run 1.16 to 1.76 times faster than AMD’s AITER on real model activations.
- Lean P, ping-pong scheduling and block scaling overlap softmax work with matrix work to close the bottleneck.
- ZYFA handles only causal forward-pass prefill and works only on MI355X.

...

## Real-world gains and accuracy

On real activations at 16K, FP8 gains reach 1.16x for Mistral-7B, 1.17x for Qwen3-8B, and 1.76x for DeepSeek-V2-Lite. On Gaussian benchmarks at 32K, the FP8 kernel with head dimension 128 achieves 2,672 TFLOP/s, compared to 1,944 for AITER. The kernel also leads on the MLA form, with 2,464 TFLOP/s versus 1,237, a ratio of 1.99.

The gap between benchmarks and real models is due to the MI355X frequency, which depends on the number of bits toggling in the operands. AITER allows more small probabilities to become zeros or subnormal numbers, which toggles fewer bits and enables a higher clock: 2,108 MHz versus 1,628 MHz for ZYFA on the Mistral-7B layer. ZYFA nevertheless requires fewer total cycles. According to the Zyphra team, performance should be measured on real activations, at sustained frequency.

Compared to an fp64 calculation, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 0.22 times that of AITER on Mistral-7B and 0.38 times on Qwen3-8B. On the full Mistral-7B model, the KL divergence, which measures the difference between two probability distributions, reaches 3.4×10⁻³ with ZYFA and 5.9×10⁻³ with AITER. Zyphra also notes that ZYFA is limited to causal forward-pass prefill, without decoding or paged KV cache, and that it only works on MI355X.

signals.title: AMD Quark adds online quantization to ROCm for vLLM, ATOM, SGLang serving engines
signals.excerpt:
AMD's Quark quantization library now supports online quantization that converts model weights during loading rather than requiring pre-exported quantized checkpoints, enabling faster iteration for RL training rollouts and mixed-precision exploration on ROCm.

## Summary

AMD has introduced online quantization to its Quark library for ROCm, allowing large language model serving engines to quantize weights at load time rather than through a separate offline export step. The feature integrates with vLLM, ATOM, and SGLang, converting high-precision checkpoints to formats like FP8 or MXFP4 layer-by-layer as weights stream into memory. This eliminates the need for calibration data, accuracy-recovery algorithms, and intermediate disk artifacts that offline quantization requires.

The technique targets specific scenarios where offline quantization proves impractical: reinforcement learning rollouts where policy weights change every step, requantization between formats such as NVFP4-to-MXFP4 without disk conversion, rapid mixed-precision scheme exploration through config edits rather than full export runs, and minor modifications to existing quantized checkpoints. AMD reports that online quantization achieves throughput parity with native offline-quantized checkpoints on models including DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-235B, though it uses round-to-nearest quantization without the accuracy-recovery techniques available offline.

## How online quantization works in ROCm serving stacks

- Layer-wise streaming conversion: Quantization occurs inside each weight-loading hook as tensors arrive, dequantizing to high precision and requantizing to the target format (FP8, MXFP4, NVFP4) one layer at a time rather than processing the entire checkpoint in memory.
- Memory bounding: Processing weights incrementally during I/O keeps peak host and device memory constrained compared to loading a full high-precision checkpoint into memory before conversion, though still higher than loading an already-quantized artifact.
- Round-to-nearest limitation: Online quantization does not support calibration data or accuracy-recovery algorithms such as rotation, SmoothQuant, GPTQ, or AWQ; it relies solely on RTN, trading accuracy optimization for pipeline simplicity and iteration speed.
- Engine integrations: AMD Quark online quantization ships with adapters for vLLM, ATOM, and SGLang serving engines, allowing deployment without modifying the underlying checkpoint storage format or maintaining multiple quantized artifacts per model.
- Requantization path: The system can consume already-quantized checkpoints in one format (e.g., NVFP4 block-scale) and convert to another target format (e.g., MXFP4) during load, demonstrated on AMD Instinct GPUs without intermediate dequantized disk storage.

...

The technique particularly benefits reinforcement learning practitioners who previously could not ... However, the absence of calibration-based accuracy recovery means production deployments requiring maximum precision will still need offline pipelines, positioning online quantization as a complementary tool rather than a replacement.

signals.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks.

The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs.

...

- Sparse attention on a hybrid model: K3.1 Pro keeps K3's KDA + MLA hybrid and adds a DSA indexer to all 24 MLA layers. At long context, a decode step reads about a quarter of the bytes per layer that dense MLA reads.
- One KV cache for three kinds of state: vLLM packs each block's MLA latent, indexer keys and KDA state together. The packed cache runs with FlashInfer and FlashMLA sparse kernels with FP8 or NVFP4 KV and optional MXFP4 index keys, and P/D disaggregation transfers it unchanged.
- Token-sharded prefill attention: up to 1.69× faster time to first token (TTFT) than head-sharded prefill at 340K tokens on 8× GB300.
- Decode context parallelism (DCP) with a sparse indexer: an exact top-k merge with ~10× less traffic makes the attention module 1.3–1.5× faster at DCP8. DCP prefill attention runs 4.1–4.3× faster per layer, and DCP8 holds 7.2× the KV tokens of TP8.
- Fused low-latency decode: the specialized CuTe DSL decode path from Kimi K3 now covers DSA layers, making decode 1.2–1.6× faster on 8× GB300, and 1.9× faster under DCP8.
- Agentic serving: on NVIDIA GB300, up to 375.9 tok/s per user at the latency-sensitive end and 37.8K total tok/s per GPU at the throughput end; on NVIDIA Rubin, up to 815.6 tok/s per user and 68.7K total tok/s per GPU on the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark.
- Zero-mismatch RL on day 0: for the first time, day-0 support comes with zero-mismatch RL: vLLM and Megatron produce bit-identical log-probs for both the base model and the LoRA adapter, so the PPO KL is exactly 0 at every step of a 100-step full-model run.

...

| KV cache per token, per GPU (24 full-attention layers) | Bytes |
| --- | --- |
| Kimi K3, FP8 MLA latent | 13,824 |
| Kimi K3.1 Pro, FP8 latent + FP8 index keys | 16,992 |
| Kimi K3.1 Pro, NVFP4 latent + MXFP4 index keys | 10,080 |

The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8.

signals.title: The Complete Guide to RAG, MCP, LangGraph, Embeddings, and Beyond - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
* **Model Routing (OpenRouter):** An abstraction layer that provides a single API to access hundreds of models, handling billing and failover automatically.
* **Local Inference (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp):** The standard for developers wanting to run open-weight models locally via a simple REST API or desktop GUI.
### Prompt Engineering and Structured Interactions
Prompt engineering is not merely "asking the AI a question." It is the discipline of constructing context, constraints, and examples to guide a probabilistic engine toward a deterministic outcome.
* **System Instructions vs. User Messages:** The system prompt sets the global behavioral boundaries. The user message contains the specific task.
* **Structured Outputs:** Modern APIs support strict JSON Schema validation. This forces the model to output valid JSON via grammar-constrained decoding, allowing application code to parse the response reliably without regex hacking.
* **Function Calling (Tool Calling):** The model does not execute code. Instead, it outputs a structured JSON request stating, "I need to call the `get\_weather` function." Your application intercepts this, executes the API call, and feeds the result back to the model.
* **Prompt Injection:** A security vulnerability where malicious user input overrides the system prompt. Defense requires strict input sanitization and separation of data from instructions.
|Category|Tool / Provider|Best Use Case|Limitations|
|**Professional API**|OpenAI / Anthropic|Production reasoning, complex agents|High token costs, data leaves your VPC|
|**Model Router**|OpenRouter|Multi-provider failover, cost optimization|Added latency, reliance on third-party routing|
|**Self-Hosted / Free**|Ollama + Llama 3|Local dev, privacy-sensitive prototyping|Requires significant RAM/VRAM, setup overhead|
|**Enterprise Cloud**|AWS Bedrock / Azure AI|Compliance, VPC integration, SLAs|Complex IAM setup, enterprise pricing|
## 4. Embeddings and Semantic Search
An embedding model translates unstructured data (text, images) into dense arrays of floating-point numbers called vectors. These vectors map the *semantic meaning* of the data into a high-dimensional geometric space.
* **Semantic Similarity:** In vector space, "canine" and "dog" are located close together, while "dog" and "automobile" are far apart.
* **Dense vs. Sparse Embeddings:** Sparse embeddings (like BM25) rely on exact keyword matching. Dense embeddings (generated by neural networks) capture contextual meaning. Modern search uses **Hybrid Search**, combining both.
* **Distance Metrics:** Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors (ignoring magnitude), making it the standard for text similarity.
* **Version Compatibility:** You cannot mix embeddings generated by `text-embedding-ada-002` with `text-embedding-3-large` in the same index. Migrating models requires re-embedding your entire dataset.
**> Crucial Distinction:
**> An embedding model
*> creates
*> the vectors. A vector database
*> stores and searches
*> them. They are entirely separate components in the stack. Embeddings are not vector databases.
### Embedding Providers Comparison
|Provider|Model Examples|Characteristics|Pricing Model|
|**OpenAI**|`text-embedding-3-large`|High accuracy, supports dimension shortening|Paid API (per token)|
|**Voyage AI**|`voyage-3`|Optimized for RAG, coding, and specific domains|Paid API|
|**Jina AI**|`jina-embeddings-v3`|Strong multilingual and long-context support|Freemium / Paid|
|**Hugging Face**|`BGE-M3` (BAAI)|Open-weight, excellent for local/hybrid search|Free (Self-hosted)|
## 5. Vector Databases and Retrieval Infrastructure
Relational databases are optimized for exact matches and complex joins. Vector databases are optimized for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search across millions of high-dimensional vectors.
* **Vector Indexing (HNSW):** Most production vector DBs use Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs. This algorithm creates multi-layered maps of the data, allowing the database to skip irrelevant vectors and find the closest matches in milliseconds.
* **Metadata Filtering:** In production, you rarely search the entire database. You search for vectors where `tenant\_id = X` and `access\_level = Y`. Vector DBs combine scalar metadata filtering with vector similarity search.
* **Multitenancy:** Enterprise systems must isolate data logically (via metadata payloads) or physically (via separate collections/namespaces) to prevent cross-tenant data leaks.
**> Crucial Distinction:
**> Vector similarity is not truth. A vector match means the text is
*> semantically related
*> to the query, not necessarily that the text is factually accurate or answers the user's specific question.
### Vector Database Comparison
|Database|Type|Best For|Limitations|
|**FAISS**|Library|In-memory local search, massive batch processing|Not a database; no native persistence or distributed scaling|
|**Chroma**|Open Source|Local development, simple Python prototypes|Struggles with massive scale and complex distributed production loads|
|**pgvector**|Postgres Ext.|Teams already using Postgres, hybrid SQL/Vector|HNSW tuning is complex; slower at massive scale than dedicated DBs|
|**Qdrant**|Open Source|High-performance production, Rust-based, filtering|Requires dedicated infrastructure or managed cloud|
|**Milvus**|Open Source|Massive, distributed enterprise-scale deployments|Complex Kubernetes deployment and operational overhead|
|**Pinecone**|Managed (SaaS)|Teams wanting zero-ops, serverless vector search|Proprietary, data leaves your VPC, can become expensive at scale|
When to use what? Use **Chroma** or **FAISS** for local Jupyter notebooks. Use **pgvector** if your dataset is under a few million rows and you already pay for a managed Postgres instance. Use **Qdrant** or **Milvus** when building dedicated, high-throughput production retrieval systems. For a deeper look at chunking strategies and RAG implementation and retrieval engineering, it is critical to evaluate retrieval independently of generation.
## 6. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Agentic RAG
LLMs suffer from knowledge cutoffs and hallucinations regarding private data. RAG solves this by retrieving relevant context from a vector database and injecting it into the LLM's prompt before generation.
### The RAG Pipeline
1. **Ingestion & Parsing:** Extracting text from PDFs, HTML, or DOCX files.
2. **Chunking:** Splitting documents into semantic or fixed-size blocks. Poor chunking destroys context.
3. **Metadata Extraction:** Tagging chunks with source URLs, dates, and author data.
4. **Embedding & Storage:** Converting chunks to vectors and saving them in the DB.
5. **Retrieval:** Searching the DB with the user's query.
6. **Reranking:** Using a Cross-Encoder model to score the top 50 retrieved chunks and select the absolute best 5 for the prompt.
7. **Generation:** The LLM answers using *only* the provided context.
**Common RAG Mistakes:** Missing authorization filters (User A retrieves User B's private document chunks), and failing to evaluate retrieval separately from answer quality. More context does not automatically produce better answers; irrelevant context confuses the model and increases token costs.
### Agentic RAG vs. Traditional RAG
Not all RAG systems are agents.
* **Traditional RAG:** A deterministic pipeline. User asks a question -> System retrieves 5 chunks -> LLM generates an answer.
* **Agentic RAG:** The LLM acts as an autonomous router. It analyzes the user's intent, decides *which* database to query, evaluates the returned data, and if the evidence is insufficient, it autonomously rewrites the query and searches again.
Agentic RAG solves complex, multi-hop questions. However, iterative retrieval introduces severe trade-offs: multiplied latency, exponential token costs, and the risk of the agent entering an infinite loop of useless searches.
## 7. AI Agents, LangChain, and LangGraph
An AI agent is an LLM embedded inside an execution loop with access to memory and external tools. An LLM is not necessarily an AI agent, and an AI agent is not simply a chatbot with a system prompt.
* **Chatbot:** Waits for user input, generates text.
* **Automated Workflow:** Follows a rigid, deterministic DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) defined by a developer. An automated workflow is not automatically an agent.
* **AI Agent:** Given a high-level goal, it plans a sequence of steps, executes tools, observes the results, handles errors, and decides when the goal is achieved.
When designing multi-step reasoning, hands-on AI agent engineering articles emphasize the importance of state management. A major challenge in multi-tool agents is handling conflicting results from AI agent tools, which requires robust fallback logic and human-in-the-loop escalations. Adding more agents to a system does not automatically improve it; multi-agent systems introduce massive complexity and debugging nightmares.
### LangChain vs. LangGraph
LangChain and LangGraph are frequently confused, but they serve fundamentally different architectural purposes. LangChain and LangGraph should not be treated as identical technologies.
* **LangChain:** A library of integrations. It provides document loaders, vector store connectors, and basic chain abstractions. It relies on DAGs and struggles with complex loops or long-running state persistence.
* **LangGraph:** A state-machine orchestration engine built on top of LangChain concepts. It models your application as a cyclic graph of Nodes and Edges. It maintains persistent state, allows agents to loop and self-correct, and supports checkpointing (pausing execution for human approval and resuming days later).
**Decision Matrix:** If your application is a straight line from Input -> Retrieve -> Generate, use basic code or LangChain. If your application requires loops, branching logic, error recovery, and human oversight, you must use LangGraph.
## 8. Model Context Protocol (MCP)
The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open standard that standardizes how AI applications connect to external data sources and tools. Before MCP, every AI framework had its own proprietary way of defining and executing "tools."
**MCP Architecture:**
* **MCP Host:** The AI application (e.g., Claude Desktop, an IDE, or a custom agent).
* **MCP Client:** The protocol layer inside the Host that maintains connections to servers.
* **MCP Server:** A lightweight service that exposes specific capabilities (Tools, Resources, Prompts) via the protocol.
**> Crucial Distinction:
**> MCP is not an AI model or an agent framework. It is a transport and discovery protocol. Function calling and MCP solve related but different integration problems; function calling is how a model requests a tool, while MCP is how the application discovers and connects to the tool server.
Reviewing MCP integrations and tool-governance patterns helps clarify how to expose local resources safely. In enterprise environments, putting authorization boundaries around AI tool calls ensures agents don't access unauthorized data, even if the MCP server exposes the tool. MCP does not bypass security; it requires strict trust management and tool permission boundaries.
## 9. AI Automation with n8n
**n8n** is a visual workflow automation platform that has heavily invested in AI nodes. It allows developers to connect webhooks, APIs, and databases to LLMs without writing boilerplate backend code.
* **AI Nodes:** n8n provides visual nodes for LLM chains, vector store retrieval, memory management, and tool execution.
* **Orchestration:** It excels at event-driven AI. For example: *Webhook receives email -> Extract text -> Embed -> Store in Pinecone -> Trigger Slack Alert.*
* **Licensing Distinction:** n8n is "fair-code" (Sustainable Use License). It is free to self-host for internal business use, but you cannot resell it as a competing SaaS product. It is not strictly OSI open-source.
Exploring n8n AI automation workflows shows how to connect triggers to LLMs visually. However, n8n is an orchestration platform, not a replacement for every backend service. If your AI logic requires complex graph state management (LangGraph) or heavy custom code, n8n becomes a bottleneck. Use n8n for integrations, routing, and business logic automation.
## 10. Production AI Engineering
Moving from prototype to production requires implementing the "boring" engineering disciplines: Observability, Evaluation, and Guardrails. A successful prototype is not necessarily production-ready.
### Observability and Tracing
You cannot debug an LLM using standard `print()` statements. You need distributed tracing to see the exact prompt, the retrieved context, the tool calls, and the latency of every step.
* **Langfuse:** The leading open-source LLM engineering platform for tracing, prompt management, and cost tracking.
* **Arize Phoenix:** Excellent for deep observability, evaluating embeddings, and detecting drift in production data.
### Evaluation (Eval)
How do you know if your RAG system is working?
* **Ragas:** Specifically evaluates RAG pipelines (Context Precision, Context Recall, Faithfulness).
* **Promptfoo:** A CLI tool for red-teaming models, testing prompt variations, and asserting JSON schema compliance.
* **DeepEval:** An open-source framework for writing unit tests for LLM outputs.
### Resilience and Guardrails
* **Semantic Caching:** Caching vector embeddings of user queries to return instant, free responses to repetitive questions.
* **Provider Failover:** For high-availability setups, building resilient multi-provider AI systems is a standard requirement to survive API outages.
* **Guardrails:** Frameworks like NeMo Guardrails that intercept user inputs and model outputs to block PII leakage, toxic language, or off-topic hallucinations.
## 11. Practical Architecture Scenarios
### Scenario 1: A Basic AI Chatbot
* **Architecture:** Frontend UI -> API Gateway -> OpenAI/Anthropic API -> Response.
* **Reality Check:** You do not need a vector database, LangChain, or an agent framework. A simple Python/Node.js HTTP wrapper with a system prompt is sufficient.
### Scenario 2: An AI Assistant for Private Company Documents
* **Architecture:** Document Ingestion (LlamaIndex) -> Chunking -> Embeddings (Voyage AI) -> Vector DB (Qdrant). User Query -> Hybrid Search -> Reranker -> LLM Generation.
* **Reality Check:** This is standard RAG. The hardest part is not the LLM; it is the document parsing (handling complex PDF tables) and strict metadata filtering for user access control.
### Scenario 3: An AI Agent Using External Systems
* **Architecture:** User Goal -> LangGraph Agent -> MCP Client -> MCP Servers (CRM, SQL Database, Jira).
* **Reality Check:** Requires robust state management.

agentic throughput per megawatt grew far faster. On SemiAnalysis AgentX, which replays recorded coding-agent sessions with real tool-call gaps and growing context, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 then delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user.

signals.title: ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration
signals.excerpt:
# ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration #

November 06, 2026 by Anshu Raina, Yao Fu, Zhang Jiejing, Peyman Razaghi, Shiksha Patel, Ravi Gupta, Deval Shah, Adeem Jassani, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Lorri Rao, Kailash Gogineni, Zhenyu Gu, Onil Gunawardana, Emad Barsoum.

...

Serving an LLM well means making a lot of choices before you know the answer. You pick an engine, a parallel layout, precisions and scheduler settings, and for disaggregated serving a split between prefill and decode. That leaves thousands of candidates, and each trial ties up one or more multi-GPU nodes for minutes. Measuring every candidate in our searches would take about 25,000 GPU-hours, so most teams try a few guesses and keep the best. A guess that misses costs you extra GPUs or a missed latency target.

ROCm InferaSim replaces most of those measurements with fast projection. It measures once per set of kernels, calculates every configuration that runs them, and an agent searches the projections instead of the hardware. Each projection takes under half a second on one CPU core. On our own AMD Instinct™ MI355X runs, 11 anchors cost 9.1 GPU-hours and cover 226 configurations that took 204 GPU-hours to measure. GPU hours go to confirming a short list. The full method and evaluation are in the InferaSim paper [1].

signals.title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.

...

NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give:

1. Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99.
2. Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU.
3. Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device.
4. No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction.
5. Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler.
6. Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant.

...

- The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
- Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
- On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an `ml.p4d.24xlarge` and $63.296000 per hour for an `ml.p5.48xlarge` in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
- At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.

signals.title: Teel: Parallel Execution for Python Agents, No Async | AI21
signals.excerpt:
In Brief

Teel is an open source Python runtime that overlaps independent IO-bound calls in code you wrote sequentially. No `async`, no `await`, no `futures`, no `gather`. Mark expensive functions with `@cacheable`, mark orchestration with `@jit`, and a magic shadow interpreter reads ahead through your bytecode, finds calls whose arguments are already known, and dispatches them on background threads before the main thread arrives. On Princeton’s Tree of Thoughts, unmodified: 83% less runtime on average, and 8.07x on the longest run. 19% faster on average than LLM-generated `async` JavaScript inside a Deep Agents coding agent. Check the repo: github.com/AI21Labs/teel

signals.title: NVIDIA Boosts Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5% On DGX Spark - Dataconomy
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA said three software optimizations raised decode throughput for Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash model by 42.5% on a single DGX Spark desktop system.

Tests across all 1,319 GSM8K questions increased throughput to 53.89 tokens per second from 37.81 tokens per second, while accuracy changed to 96.82% from 96.89%, a statistically undetectable difference, NVIDIA said.

The test used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has a native 256,000-token context window.

DGX Spark uses NVIDIA’s GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip and has 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. NVIDIA rates the system for inference on models with as many as 200 billion parameters and says it can deliver up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4 computing performance.

NVIDIA profiled the model at batch size one and found decoding was constrained by memory reads, particularly in mixture-of-experts computation and the language-model output head. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe, using FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 language-model head.

...

The first change replaced FlashInfer’s MoE backend with Humming, an independent kernel library that compiles kernels at runtime for specific matrix shapes, data types and GPUs. NVIDIA said the change supported the model’s narrow 768-wide expert layer and increased throughput by 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second.

The second change applied FP8 quantization to the language-model head at load time. The head is a 157,184-by-2,560 BF16 matrix, and NVIDIA said FP8 halves the memory reads required for that layer. Humming combined with the FP8 head reached 43.94 tokens per second, up 21.7% from baseline.

The third change used multi-token prediction speculative decoding through Ling-3.0-flash’s built-in NEXTN prediction layer, eliminating the need for a separate draft model. On the synthetic test, 3.90 tokens were accepted per round and throughput rose to 102.88 tokens per second, a 185.1% increase from baseline.

...

With all three changes enabled on GSM8K, time per output token fell to 18.56 milliseconds from 26.45 milliseconds. Mean latency declined 24.5% to 11.49 seconds from 15.21 seconds.
